p.title: Conflating Lobbying and PACs: The Surprisingly Low Overlap in Organizational Lobbying and Campaign Expenditures
p.venue: Political Science (journal name from running header; full venue not confirmed)

ext.title: Conflating Lobbying and PACs: The Surprisingly Low Overlap in Organizational Lobbying and Campaign Expenditures
ext.venue: PS: Political Science & Politics (Cambridge University Press on behalf of the American Political Science Association), October 2025, pp. 597-605, "Politics" section. Metadata hint corrected: the journal is PS: Political Science & Politics, confirmed by the copyright line, running footer and data-availability statement.
ext.document_type: Research article (short empirical, descriptive; PDF has 9 pages, journal pp. 597-605, including references)
ext.coverage: Full text read in one pass (the Read call returned all 853 lines, through journal p. 605, with no truncation). Scope touched: lobbying, PACs, access, revolving-door lobbying, PAC timing, legislators (committee access, foreign lobbyists), and the 2008 HLOGA disclosure law. Not covered by the paper: path-finding, allocation models, networks as a method, turnout or persuasion, and text measurement.
ext.research_question: Are campaign contributions (PAC giving) and lobbying complements, substitutes, or unrelated forms of organizational political engagement? Empirically: how much do the interest groups that lobby overlap with the groups that contribute through PACs, and which types of organizations do each?
ext.theory: Access-purchase account: PAC contributions open doors that lobbyists then use, so PAC givers should also lobby and heavy lobbyists should have PACs. Election-targeting account: contributions mainly aim at electoral outcomes, so the two activities need not be linked; organizations can also lobby without donating. The authors treat the two as conceptually distinct: lobbying involves no direct transfer to members, while contributions do. They explicitly do not theorize why organizations choose one, both, or neither.
ext.data: Center for Responsive Politics (CRP) data, curated from LDA Registrations and Activity Reports (LaPira and Thomas 2020) and FEC contribution disclosures by organizations and their officially affiliated PACs, linked by an expert-curated CRP crosswalk. Unit: organization (interest group). Period: 1998-2018 (even-numbered cycles in the figures). Sample sizes stated in the text: 9,076 organizations reporting political involvement in 1998; 15,729 in the 2008 cycle (text: "a decade later"). Figure 4 pooled counts over 1998-2018: Only Lobbies n=34,038; Only Contributes n=9,528; Lobbies and Contributes n=3,427; Not Active n=7,524 (sum 54,517, computed by the extractor). Lobbying totals include in-house and contract-firm lobbyists. Figure 1 cycle-level bar labels did not parse cleanly from the text layer, so only the figures stated in the prose are used here.
ext.method: Descriptive only. Figure 1: yearly share of organizations that are lobby-only, PAC-only, or both. Figure 2: share of yearly lobbying expenditures and of PAC contributions by group type. Figure 3: distributions of average yearly PAC contributions (3a) and average yearly lobbying spending (3b) by group type, shown as dot plots with violin density, mean, IQR and 2.5/97.5 percentiles. Figure 4: log-log scatter of total lobbying spending against total PAC contributions per organization, with marginal histograms, coloured by the four activity categories. No regression, hypothesis test, or model is reported.
ext.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim and uses no identification strategy; it is a descriptive accounting of overlap.
ext.scope: Population: US federal interest-group organizations that register to lobby under the LDA or are PAC or political-committee filers in CRP data, 1998-2018. Institution: Congress (lobbying) and federal candidate elections (contributions). Excluded by design: independent expenditures and Super PACs (note 1, p. 604); dark-money contributions (unobserved by definition, p. 599); contributions by employees and contract lobbyists, which are not counted as organizational giving (p. 599).

key_findings.finding: Most politically active organizations engage in only one of the two activities; only a small minority do both. The abstract states the headline finding, and the results section gives the counts.
key_findings.numbers: 1998 (n=9,076 orgs): 24% PAC-only, 64% lobby-only, 12% both. Around 2008 (n=15,729 orgs): 20% PAC-only, 70% lobby-only, 10% both. Percentages in each year sum to 100, so the categories are treated as exclusive.

key_findings.finding: Pooled over 1998-2018, only a small share of organizations do both.
key_findings.numbers: Lobby-only ~34,000 (n=34,038); PAC-only ~9,500 (n=9,528); registered but not active ~7,500 (n=7,524); both n=3,427 = 6.3% of the 54,517 total (6.3% is stated in the text; the 54,517 denominator is the extractor's sum).

key_findings.finding: Lobbying money is concentrated among organizations that also make PAC contributions, but that share fell over time.
key_findings.numbers: About 75% of lobbying expenditures (1998-2018) came from organizations that also contributed through PACs. The share of PAC contributions coming from organizations that also lobby fell from more than 65% in 1998 to about 30% in 2018.

key_findings.finding: Organizations that both lobby and contribute spend far more on lobbying than lobby-only organizations.
PAC contributions are higher on average among dual-activity organizations, and the distribution is very wide.
key_findings.numbers: Contribute-only: mean $7,857 (IQR $2,000-$33,566). Both: mean $31,167 (IQR $8,227-$1,082,366). The largest average contributors exceed $100 million (examples named: Crossroads GPS, Restore Our Future, Priorities USA).

key_findings.finding: The top lobbying groups spend the most and almost always have affiliated PACs, so most lobbying money comes from a few big spenders that also have PACs.
key_findings.numbers: No separate numeric estimate beyond the Figure 2 and Figure 3 results above.

key_findings.finding: Lobbying spending starts high and concentrates between $10,000 and $1 million, while PAC spending is more uneven, with many contributors giving under $10,000.
key_findings.numbers: Few lobbying organizations report under $10,000. Many PAC givers are under $10,000.

key_findings.finding: The authors restate the overlap as a yearly figure and note that organizations doing both are likely better resourced and, on average, more conservative. The conservatism point is cited to Crosson, Furnas and Lorenz (2020), not tested here.
key_findings.numbers: Only a 10% to 15% overlap between lobbying-registered and contributing organizations in any given year.

limitations: Only contributions to candidates are counted. Independent expenditures and Super PACs are excluded (note 1, p. 604).
Dark-money contributions are not observed, by definition, because they are unaffiliated with disclosing organizations (p. 599).
Contributions by employees and contract lobbyists are not counted as organizational giving (p. 599). The paper says individual lobbyist donations need further study (p. 603-604).

Possible undercounting of lobbying organizations with PACs because of lax LDA reporting and enforcement. The authors argue that shadow-lobbyist gaps sit at the individual level, not the organization level (note 3, p. 604).

Purely descriptive. The paper does not test why organizations choose one, both, or neither, and says it did not speculate about motivations (p. 599). It calls for future work on that question (p. 599, p. 604).
The authors note that individual corporate-executive giving, including to Super PACs, is not analyzed (p. 604).
Figure 1 cycle-level counts were not reliably recoverable from the text layer; the prose figures are used instead.
measures: Organization activity category: lobby-only, PAC-only, both (lobbies and contributes), registered but not active (Figure 4 categories).
Lobbying spending: LDA expenditure totals including in-house and contract-firm lobbyists; yearly and total 1998-2018.
PAC contributions: candidate contributions by the organization or its officially affiliated PAC; yearly and total.
Yearly activity share by category (Figure 1) and share of spending by group type (Figure 2).
Distributional summaries: mean, IQR, 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of average yearly PAC contributions and lobbying spending by category.

short_quotes.quote: minimal overlap between organizations that engage in lobbying and those that make campaign contributions

paul_markup.text: Abstract: lobbying and PAC giving show minimal overlap, though the public treats them as one 'money in politics'.
Only a small share of organizations do both; this challenges the assumption that the two are inherently linked.
The top lobbying groups spend the most and almost always have affiliated PACs.
The public does not distinguish lobbying spending from campaign contributions.
Press framing that Trump's resort memberships and donor events made him accessible to lobbyists.
Press account of Harris's 'open-door' posture toward lobbyists and industry fundraising for her campaign.
Media coverage blurs the line between lobbying and campaign donations.
The 2008 HLOGA law makes LDA-registered lobbyists report contributions under a 'lobbying disclosure' heading, conflating the two.
Lobbyist contribution disclosure goes to the House Clerk and Senate Secretary, not the FEC, and those officials lack enforcement authority.
Disclosures do not show whether lobbyists' donations are protected speech or de facto quid pro quo spending.
The authors call for conceptual and empirical clarification, since the basic premise has no clear record behind it.
Lobbying involves no direct transfer of money to members; campaign contributions do.
Restatement of the main result: remarkably little overlap between lobbying and contributing organizations.
Interest-group PACs give to members who work on their issues, and generally not to first-term legislators.
Foreign lobbyists often seek access to legislators they have donated to (Liu 2022).
Contribution timing points to both election outcomes and congressional voting: more money in election years and when issues are on the agenda.
Theory: if PAC giving is access-oriented, PAC organizations should lobby and lobbying organizations should have PACs.
Lobbying can be influential in notice-and-comment rulemaking (Dwidar 2022), despite mixed evidence on legislation.
High lobbying returns are more likely when firms use revolving-door lobbyists with strong networks in Congress.
Lobbying success may depend more on lobbyist-Congress relationships than on the firm's PAC giving.
Only a small minority of interest groups engage in both activities.
An anonymous lobbyist's interview shows that the choice to lobby or contribute is strategic and deliberate.
Future research should ask why and when organizations choose some activities and forgo others.
Data scope: only organizational and officially affiliated PAC donations are counted, not those of employees or contract lobbyists.
Political activity in the 2014-2018 period levels off, though still higher than in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Figure 1 breakdown, 2008 cycle: the PAC-only share of politically active organizations.
Figure 1 breakdown, 2008 cycle: the lobby-only share (about 70%) and the both-activity share (about 10%).
Average PAC contributions vary widely across organizations, with the largest averages above $100 million.
Implications: the term 'money in politics' lumps together distinct influence strategies, so many groups focus on lobbying.
PAC spending is uneven, with many contributors giving under $10,000, unlike lobbying spending.
Lobbying is an ongoing commitment that runs for months or years, given the long policy-making process.
Researchers should not conflate lobbying with electioneering, since the two rarely coincide outside the most prominent players.
Lobbyists' fundraisers build relationships and are an initial, polite step toward future access.

rel.summary_md:
Furnas, LaPira and Brock (PS, Oct 2025) put Center for Responsive Politics LDA lobbying records and FEC records of organization and affiliated-PAC giving side by side for each organization, 1998-2018. Most politically active organizations do only one of the two. In 1998 (n=9,076 organizations), 64% only lobbied, 24% only gave through a PAC and 12% did both. By 2008 (n=15,729) the split was 70/20/10. Pooled over 1998-2018, 3,427 of 54,517 organizations (6.3%) did both. That denominator is the extractor's sum of the Figure 4 counts.

Within that minority sits most of the lobbying money. About 75% of lobbying spending in 1998-2018 came from organizations that also gave through a PAC. Their mean yearly lobbying spend was $403k, against $64k for organizations that only lobbied. Going the other way, the share of PAC dollars that came from lobbying organizations fell from over 65% in 1998 to about 30% in 2018. Employee giving, Super PACs and dark money are excluded. The paper is purely descriptive: no model, no identification strategy, and nothing about access or votes.

For Paul's systems the paper matters in three ways:

- **FEC as a stand-in for lobbying.** Across the population, campaign money is a poor proxy for lobbying. That supports the twice-locked rule that FEC exposure is never presented as a lobbying predictor. It also argues against reading the 42-month figure as a lead time: in the code it is only how much fresher the FEC data is than the LDA data.
- **The flip model's competitor-money leg.** That leg counts only PAC money. It can see the large trade associations, which almost all have PACs. It cannot see organizations that lobby without a PAC.
- **Mentat's counts.** Mentat matches individual employee giving by employer string. The paper's definition of organizational giving excludes employees, so its overlap figures do not carry over to Mentat's totals without first aligning the two definitions.

bearings.paper_claim: Organizations that lobby and organizations that give through PACs barely overlap. Per year: 1998 (n=9,076 organizations) 64% lobby only, 24% PAC only, 12% both; 2008 (n=15,729) 70/20/10. Pooled 1998-2018: 3,427 of 54,517 organizations (6.3%) do both; the denominator is the extractor's sum. The authors put the yearly overlap at 10-15% and warn researchers not to conflate lobbying with electioneering.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.597; Results pp.600-601; Figure 4 p.603; Implications p.603-604
bearings.system_side: Bridge round 3 is closed. At member level the raw correlation was rho +0.153, but the four-control partial was -0.0002, over 2023-2026 with N=213 pairs (fintech and crypto, two cycles each). The binding product rule says FEC exposure is never a lobbying predictor, and the bridge only paired the 22 locked lob_ids that appear in both the FEC and the LDA data.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is about organizations and the bridge test is about members (where money and lobbying attention land). They are different estimands. The paper does not explain the partial of zero, which came from structural co-targeting. What carries over is the population-level point: for the 64-70% of organizations that lobby without a PAC there is no FEC signal at all, so FEC cannot work as a general lobbying proxy. The bridge's 22-lob_id crosswalk was selected on organizations doing both, which is the 6-15% minority, so its null does not extend to organizations that only lobby. The paper covers federal organizations, 1998-2018, under CRP definitions. UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Most lobbying organizations make no PAC contributions (64-70% lobby only). The share of PAC dollars coming from organizations that also lobby fell from more than 65% (1998) to about 30% (2018). Employee giving is not organizational giving.
bearings.paper_location: Results pp.600-601 (Figure 2 text); data scope p.599
bearings.system_side: The 'FEC leads LDA by 42 months' candidate heuristic comes from lead_months, which is computed as the gap between the latest FEC transaction date and the end of the LobbyView year. That is a measure of how much fresher the FEC data is, not an estimated lag. The FEC source here is employee and executive itemized giving from a 10-company sample per industry.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's low overlap undercuts any reading in which one organization's giving foreshadows its own later lobbying, because most lobbying organizations do not give. It speaks to organizational PAC money, not to the employee giving this prior uses, so it bounds the lead claim rather than refuting it. The freshness reading of lead_months is unaffected. UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: About 75% of 1998-2018 lobbying expenditures came from organizations that also gave through PACs. The top lobbying spenders almost always have affiliated PACs, and organizations doing both average $403k a year in lobbying vs $64k for lobby-only organizations. Even so, most lobbying organizations (64-70% yearly) make no PAC contributions.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.597; Results p.601 (Figures 2, 3b); Implications p.602
bearings.system_side: The competitor (b) leg of pflip enters opposing-industry pressure only as PAC money: ind0 = banks + finserv from congestion.json, saturated relative to receipts, with WM 0.35 vs WP 0.65. No lobbying-spend channel feeds b.
bearings.transfer_conditions: For finance, the large opponents (ABA, ICBA, big banks) are exactly the dual-activity heavy spenders, so PAC money flags the biggest lobbying forces reasonably well. It misses fintech and crypto organizations that lobby without a PAC. The paper says nothing about whether money buys access or votes, so it gives no support to the WM/WP split. UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Organizational giving is defined as candidate contributions from the organization or its officially affiliated PAC. Contributions by employees and by contract lobbyists are explicitly not counted. Super PACs, independent expenditures and dark money are excluded.
bearings.system_side: Mentat attributes Schedule A individual receipts to roster companies by matching normalized employer strings, so its 'industry giving' includes employee giving that the paper excludes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Any comparison of Mentat's industry totals or participation counts with the paper's overlap or distribution figures (for example, many PAC givers under $10k) has to restrict Mentat to organizational and affiliated-PAC receipts first. The precognition memo already records that employee giving and industry PAC money are different instruments, with lean signs agreeing in only 57% of members (157/276).

bearings.paper_claim: Lobbying and PAC spending have different populations and distributions. Few organizations report lobbying under $10k, and most spend $10k-$1M; PAC giving is uneven, with many givers under $10k. Lobbying is an ongoing commitment over months or years. The authors argue against treating the two as one 'money in politics' figure.
bearings.system_side: Mentat keeps LDA lobbying levels in their own card, separate from the giving forecast. Outside-firm income and in-house expenses are shown side by side and never added.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports keeping giving and lobbying as separate measures with separate models. It does not speak to the in-house vs outside-firm no-sum rule, which is about LDA double counting. CRP data does deduplicate that, and Mentat's sector-growth config separately notes a 9-26% double count in undifferentiated LobbyView sums (sgs_config.R:119). The evidence is descriptive.

gaps_exposed: There is no census, by organization, of who lobbies only, who gives through a PAC only, and who does both, for the CU, bank, fintech and crypto opponent sets. So the system cannot say how much of the opposition's lobbying force is invisible to the PAC-only money channel in the flip and money-response models.

The flip model's competitor leg (flip_model.py:39) has no lobbying-intensity term. Organizations that lobby without a PAC (64-70% of lobbying organizations in the paper's data) add nothing to b. Any fix would need a lobbying-spend source other than LDA member edges (D-021). The paper does not say how to weight such a source, and this is a gap, not a recommendation.

The opposition prior and Mentat use employee giving, while the paper and congestion.json use organizational and affiliated-PAC giving. No reconciliation sits between the two definitions, and the paper shows the definition decides who counts as 'giving' at all.

LD-203 lobbyist contribution reports (the HLOGA channel the paper says conflates lobbying with giving) are used only to resolve a registrant's identity (fec/surfaces/build_staffer_groups_section.py:907). That is consistent with D-021. The system does not measure contributions from individual lobbyists, which the paper flags as understudied.
flags: The '42-month lead' (FEC leads LDA) is computed in build_opposition_prior.py:564-572 as a data-freshness gap, not an estimated lead. The paper's 64-70% lobby-only share argues against any wording that implies an organization's FEC giving foreshadows its own lobbying. That is consistent with the twice-locked rule that FEC exposure is never a lobbying predictor.

Paul's position list cites this paper under flip-model as support for 'money buys access'. The paper tests neither access nor votes: it is descriptive overlap only. It must not be cited as support for the WM 0.35 / WP 0.65 split or for any access claim.
LDA stays an identity source (D-021). The paper's discussion of HLOGA LD-203 contribution reporting is not a licence to turn LD-203 contributions into member edges or weights.

Overlap figures must keep their windows and denominators. Per year: 12% (1998, n=9,076) and 10% (2008, n=15,729). Pooled: 6.3% of 54,517 organizations, 1998-2018; that denominator is the extractor's sum of the Figure 4 counts, not printed in the paper. The 75% lobbying-dollar share is pooled over 1998-2018.
Every bearing here is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's highlights (low overlap, 'do not conflate lobbying with electioneering', the top lobbying groups almost always have PACs) agree with where the system now stands. Bridge round 3 found a four-control partial of zero, and the standing rule bars FEC exposure as a lobbying predictor. His fec-lda-bridge position is right that his own notes expected donations to lead lobbying, and that expectation is stale. On 2026-07-31 he ratified FEC as a 'precognition' heuristic for lobbying attention, and the 42-month figure that came out of that is a freshness gap, not a lead. His flip-model entry cites the paper alongside 'money buys access', but the paper is silent on access and votes. The only relevant thing it shows is that PAC money identifies the large dual-activity spenders and misses organizations that lobby without a PAC. His election-year timing highlight comes from the paper's literature review, not from its own findings. So for mentat-giving-forecast.cycle-model it is context only, not evidence. His annotation record for this paper has no takeaways, system links or cross-refs filled in.

related.why: Kim et al. find firm-level sequential links between donations and lobbying among large firms. Furnas et al. show that firms doing both are a 6-15% minority, so those links describe the dual-activity elite, not the population.
This is the later version of the sequential-links argument. It is fully consistent with Furnas only if its sample is restricted to organizations that both lobby and give.
Furnas cites Kalla & Broockman 2016 as experimental evidence that contributions buy access. That is the access account their overlap data puts in context.
Same first author. The moneyed-interests experiment (Furnas et al. 2023, PRQ) is cited as contrary evidence on buying access.
Studies corporate lobbying and PACs together in relation to market concentration. Furnas supplies the base rate for how often firms use both.
Paul's cross-industry finance and lobbying memo puts both spending types side by side. Furnas warns that they come from largely different organization populations and should not be added together.
A cross-industry political-spending overview. Furnas's definitional limits (organizational PAC vs employee giving, no Super PACs) decide how its totals can be compared.
